title: The Robbed Coach
subtitle: Monday 14 to Saturday 19 November 1864: A Notice on a Door, Washing on a Line, Guns at the Elbow

setting.name: Ninebark and the Bannack road, the week of the fourth robbery
setting.description: The party arrives in Ninebark on the Monday up coach, four days after the committee hanged Patrick Kehoe, and is hired by the Beaverhead Express Company to ride guard on Thursday's down coach, which carries $38,000 in dust. The week establishes the camp, the committee's fear, the express company's desperation and the road. On Thursday the coach is stopped at the Elbow on the Rattlesnake Grade, and the party fights road agents on a shelf of frozen road with a cliff on one side. On Friday the committee wants witnesses, and names. On Friday night a card is pushed under a door. If the party took a road agent alive, the committee comes for him on Saturday night.
setting.atmosphere: Bright, hard cold: blue sky, snow on the peaks, frost on everything in the morning, mud frozen into ruts. The camp works all day and goes silent after dark. On the road the cold is worse: the coach's leather curtains crack when they are rolled, the horses' breath freezes on their whiskers, the driver's horn is the loudest sound for miles. Fiddler's Station is warm, loud and welcoming, with a stove, a pot of venison stew and a cheerful host. The grade is a white shelf above a drop, with dark timber below and the sound of the creek under ice.

keyLocations.name: Water Street and Wexford's store
keyLocations.description: The heart of Ninebark: Obadiah Wexford's two-storey store, with its plate-glass windows hauled over the mountains from Salt Lake City, a long counter, gold scales at both ends, barrels of flour and nails, and a big stove with chairs round it where half the camp's business is done. The committee's printed notice is on the door. Behind the store is Wexford's warehouse, and under the warehouse a root cellar with a padlocked door, where Jack Tillery was kept.
features: The notice: TO THE PEOPLE OF NINEBARK. THE NAMES ARE KNOWN. LET THE GUILTY LEAVE THIS CAMP WHILE THEY STILL CAN. BY ORDER, THE COMMITTEE OF VIGILANCE. Printed on the Sentinel's press; Jonas Fenley printed it and says he had no choice
The stove circle: a dozen men talking about the hangings in low voices, and stopping when strangers come in
Wexford's ledger of who owes him, and his gold scales, which are honest
The root cellar door behind the warehouse, padlocked, with fresh scratches on the inside of the frame
encounters: Sheriff Barnabas Wyndham, standing in front of the notice, who introduces himself to any armed stranger and asks them, politely, which side they are on
Obadiah Wexford, who welcomes newcomers warmly and asks them to dinner, because the committee wants to know who they are
secrets: The committee's members watch the street. Anyone who talks to Barnabas Wyndham for more than a few minutes in public is noticed (WATCH +0, but Grimsby asks about them by name on Friday).

Wexford is the committee's president and founder. He is not wearing a mask in daylight; nobody in camp says so, and everybody knows. Insight DC 13 in conversation: he is frightened and badly wants someone to tell him he did the right thing.

keyLocations.name: The Beaverhead Express office
keyLocations.description: A small, solid building of squared logs on Water Street with a brick vault at the back, iron bars on the window and the company's name in gilt. Simeon Prothero, the agent, weighs the miners' dust on a big balance, seals it in buckskin pokes, enters each shipper's name and weight on a waybill, and locks the pokes in the iron-bound treasure boxes for the Thursday coach. Three robberies and a dead messenger have aged him ten years in a month; the company's superintendent in Salt Lake City has told him one more robbery will cost him his post.
features: The waybill book: every shipment since May, by shipper and weight; the Thursday coaches of 13 October, 20 October and 3 November all carried more than $20,000, and were all robbed; the coaches of 27 October and 10 November carried under $8,000 and were not
The treasure boxes: green-painted, iron-bound, with two padlocks, about seventy pounds empty; $38,000 in dust weighs about a hundred and thirty pounds more
A framed photograph of Will Danforth and Benicio Aranda on the box of a coach, taken in Bannack in August, on the wall behind the counter
encounters: Simeon Prothero, who hires the party on Tuesday
Benicio Aranda, if he is not played, oiling a coach gun
secrets: CLUE D1 (partial, for anyone who reads the waybill book with Prothero's permission: Investigation DC 12, or automatic with Barnabas Wyndham's ledger): the road agents always know which Thursday coach is heavy. Prothero has asked himself who knew, and the answer is: himself, the shippers, the driver, the messenger, and anyone who sees or lifts the boxes on the road. The boxes are carried off and back on at Fiddler's Station while the teams are changed, because the coach is lighter for the hostlers to handle; that has been the company's custom on the Bannack road since June.
Prothero refused to join the committee, and Grimsby and Pottinger have begun saying he is the inside man. He knows it. He is not.

keyLocations.name: Fiddler's Station
keyLocations.description: At the top of the pass, eleven miles from Ninebark: a long log house with a stone chimney and a covered porch, a big barn with a hayloft door facing the road, corrals for thirty horses, a smithy shed, a well, and a washing line strung between the porch and the barn. The coach changes horses here going both ways, and the passengers eat. Warrick Sefton keeps it with a hostler called Jemmy, a Kansas boy of sixteen, and a cook. Sefton is a big, broad, ruddy man with a laugh you can hear across the yard, who knows every driver and messenger by name, keeps a pot of venison stew on the stove day and night, and will not take a traveller's money on a cold day.
features: The washing line between the porch and the barn. On Thursday 17 November there are two red flannel shirts and a red blanket on it, frozen stiff. On Monday 14 November there was nothing
The barn: thirty stalls, harness, a hayloft, and a plank floor that sounds hollow at the back, under a pile of feed sacks
The station register, where drivers sign in and out with the time, and Sefton notes 'boxes off' and 'boxes on'
A pair of French field glasses hanging on a nail by the door, 'for watching the weather come in'
encounters: Warrick Sefton, delighted to meet the party, who asks them all about themselves and remembers every answer
Jemmy the hostler, who changes the horses, carries the boxes into the house and back while the passengers eat, and does not look anyone in the eye
secrets: CLUE D5 (Perception DC 14 for anyone who looks round the yard on Thursday; automatic for anyone who asks why a man would hang washing out in this cold): two red shirts and a red blanket on the line on a Thursday morning in November, frozen solid. Benicio Aranda, if asked, frowns: 'There was washing on that line the last time too. I remember thinking it was a strange day to wash.' The line is plain from the ridge above the Rattlesnake Grade. Nobody in the party should be told what it means; they should be left to wonder.

Sefton lifts each treasure box himself when Jemmy carries them in, 'to show the boy how', and says something cheerful about how heavy the camp's luck is running this week. Insight DC 15: he is weighing it.
Sefton is committee number 23. He will not say so, but if the party talks about the hangings he speaks of the committee with sorrowful approval: 'Hard times, hard men. I'd rather it wasn't needed.'

keyLocations.name: The Rattlesnake Grade and the Elbow
keyLocations.description: Below Fiddler's the road drops three miles to the ford of Rattlesnake Creek on a shelf cut into the mountainside: a cliff of grey rock on the uphill side, timber falling away steeply on the downhill side, room for one coach and no more. Halfway down is the Elbow, a hairpin where the road turns back on itself round a buttress of rock, and the coach must slow to a walk. All three robberies happened between the Elbow and the ford.
features: At the Elbow, the road's uphill side is a jumble of boulders where a man with a rifle can lie unseen twenty feet above the coach
Below the road, the timber is steep enough that a rider must lead his horse, and thick enough to hide five horses fifty yards away
A spruce, felled across the road just below the Elbow on the morning of 17 November, still bleeding sap: the road agents' gate
Danforth's blood is still on a boulder at the ford, under the snow, where he fell off the box on 3 November
encounters: The road agents, on Thursday 17 November (act 2)
secrets: CLUE D2 (core, for anyone who follows the road agents' tracks: Survival DC 13, or automatic with a Scout's Trailcraft or Ada Brockway): the riders came down through the timber from above and went back up it, toward the pass and Fiddler's Station, not down toward the ford and the Beaverhead Crossing. Survival DC 16, or Trailcraft: the horses are shod with a toe clip, a small lip of iron turned up at the front of the shoe, and Gabriel Tennant is the only smith in the district who makes them so. A cast shoe can be found in the timber with a DC 14 Investigation check. Gabriel identifies it at once as his own work, and his account book says which string he made that pattern for: the express company's horses at Fiddler's.

The tracks are lost in the trampled ground round Fiddler's corral, a mile and a half above. Following them there is the obvious next step; it should feel strange that a gang would ride up to a stage station, and Sefton will explain it before he is asked: 'Saw riders cut across above the barn about noon. Thought they were hunters. Should've known.'

keyLocations.name: Moira Kehoe's boarding house and the Number Three claim
keyLocations.description: A two-storey log house on Water Street with a porch, eight rooms, a kitchen that is always warm and a parlour with a piano nobody can play. Moira Kehoe keeps it alone now. Leonie Fairbairn rooms here; so do two miners, a German assayer and, from Monday, the party if they want it. A mile below town, the Number Three claim is a deep shaft in the creek gravel with a windlass house and a stove, where Patrick Kehoe worked the night shift.
features: The front door, where a committee card was pushed under on 12 November, and the kitchen table where Moira keeps it under the sugar tin
The kitchen, where the committee took Patrick at midnight on 10 November; one chair is still broken
The Number Three's windlass house, where the night shift's tally board shows who worked which nights, chalked and never wiped
encounters: Moira Kehoe, who offers rooms and says nothing about Patrick unless she is asked
The Number Three night shift: six Irish miners, frightened, who will talk only in the windlass house with the door shut
secrets: CLUE A1 (core, for anyone who asks Moira or the Number Three men where Patrick was on 3 November): the night shift of 2 to 3 November ran from six in the evening to six in the morning; Patrick was there all night with six men, who are named on the tally board. They told the committee. Grimsby wrote down that they were 'Irish and therefore unreliable'.

CLUE A2 (core, from Moira, or Leonie Fairbairn if she is played, whose room is next to the Kehoes'): Patrick came home at half past six on the morning of 3 November and slept until noon. The robbery was at about ten, fourteen miles away. Leonie heard him snoring through the wall, 'like a sawmill'.

CLUE A3 (from Konrad Kranzler if he is played; otherwise Moira knows he wrote a different certificate): the true cause of Patrick's death, 'strangulation at the hands of persons unknown', torn out by Grimsby; Konrad's own notebook has the original wording. Konrad's examination of Will Danforth also shows the fatal shot came from above and to the right at about sixty yards, which is the rocks above the Elbow: a rifleman, not a man on the road.

synopsis: The party rides into Ninebark on Monday 14 November and reads the committee's notice on Wexford's door. Simeon Prothero of the Beaverhead Express Company, who has lost three shipments and a messenger and is about to lose his post, hires them on Tuesday to ride guard on Thursday's down coach with $38,000 in dust. Barnabas Wyndham, the district's schoolmaster sheriff, asks them to bring him any road agent they take alive, to a cell and not a rope. Moira Kehoe, whose husband was hanged four days ago, gives them rooms. On Thursday the coach stops at Fiddler's Station, where the warm and generous station keeper Warrick Sefton feeds the passengers and lifts the treasure boxes, and where two red shirts and a red blanket hang frozen on the washing line. At the Elbow on the Rattlesnake Grade a felled spruce blocks the road, a rifleman in the rocks shoots the near leader, and three masked road agents come out of the timber. Whatever happens in the fight, the tracks go back up the mountain toward the station, and the horses wear a blacksmith's signature on their shoes. On Friday the committee's lawyer, Horatio Grimsby, interviews the party as witnesses and makes it plain that the committee would like a name, preferably a Missourian's. On Friday night a warning card is pushed under Leonie Fairbairn's door. If the party captured a road agent, the committee comes to take him from the district jail on Saturday night, and the party must decide whether a guilty man is worth defending from a mob.
hook: The notice on Wexford's door, Monday noon, and a thin grey man with a tin star standing in front of it. 'Barnabas Wyndham,' he says, 'sheriff of this district, for what that is presently worth. You are armed, and new, and the coach you came on has been robbed three times. I would be grateful to know whether you are here to rob it, to guard it, or to join the people who wrote this.' He taps the notice. 'I should tell you that only one of those three is legal.'

clues: A1: the Number Three night shift tally board and its six men (the windlass house)
A2: he was asleep at the boarding house from half past six until noon on 3 November (Moira, Leonie)
A3: Konrad Kranzler's original certificate, torn out by Grimsby (Konrad's notebook)

conclusions.conclusion: D. The road agents work out of Fiddler's Station (begun here; finished in vg-scenario-002)
clues: D1: the waybill book and the custom of moving the boxes at Fiddler's (the express office)
D2: the tracks go back up toward the station, on Gabriel Tennant's toe-clip shoes (the Elbow, the forge)
D5: washing on the line on robbery Thursdays (Fiddler's Station)

conclusions.conclusion: B. Tillery's confession was coached (begun here)
clues: B1: Tillery's last words to Gabriel Tennant, if the party earns Gabriel's trust this early (the forge)

acts.title: Monday and Tuesday: The Notice and the Offer
acts.description: The party arrives, meets the law, the express company, the committee's president and the widow, and is hired. The point of this act is to make the camp's fear felt and to show the players every faction before Thursday: Barnabas and the law, Prothero and the gold, Wexford and the committee, Moira and the cost. Let the players wander; the camp is small and everyone in it wants to know who they are.
objectives: Find out what the committee is and what it has done
Accept Prothero's offer to ride guard on Thursday's coach, or find another reason to be on it
Meet Barnabas Wyndham, Moira Kehoe and Gabriel Tennant
Learn where Patrick Kehoe was on the night of 2 to 3 November
encounters: A drunk Missourian (Drunk Cowboy stats) and two Union men (Saloon Brawler) start a fight in the Union Saloon on Monday night over a toast to Jefferson Davis; brawling rules, nobody meant to die, and Mordecai Pottinger watching from behind the bar to see who takes which side

scenes.name: The Notice on Wexford's Door
scenes.description: Barnabas Wyndham meets the party at the notice. Let him explain, briefly and precisely, what has happened: three robberies, Will Danforth dead, the committee founded in Wexford's store, Jack Tillery hanged on 6 November after naming names, Patrick Kehoe hanged on 10 November. He does not know the names on the list or the members of the committee, and says so: 'I asked. I was told it was for my own protection.' Then Wexford comes out of the store, shakes everyone's hand and invites them to dinner, and Barnabas goes quiet. If Cormac Hartigan is played, Barnabas has been told to expect him (Prothero told him), and is so relieved he nearly embraces him; Wexford, overhearing the word 'federal', goes very still. Insight DC 14: Wexford has heard Hartigan's name before, and it frightened him.
scenes.readAloud: The notice is printed, in good black type, on the Sentinel's best paper, and somebody has already torn one corner and stuck it back with a tack. A dozen people are reading it. Nobody is saying anything. In front of it stands a thin, stooped man in spectacles and a coat too thin for the weather, with a tin star on his lapel and his arms folded, as though by standing there long enough he might make the words go away. He sees you, and looks at your guns, and then at your faces, and unfolds his arms. Behind him the door of the store opens and a big, prosperous, white-whiskered man in a good black coat comes out, beaming, with his hand already out to shake. 'Strangers! Welcome to Ninebark. Obadiah Wexford. You'll take dinner with me, I hope; we like to know our neighbours here.' The thin man with the star says nothing at all.

skillChecks.success: Wexford's welcome is genuine and so is his fear. He wants to know who you are because he wants to know whether you are a threat to the camp, and the committee asked him to find out. Barnabas Wyndham is not a coward, though he looks it: he has decided to be seen standing there every day.
skillChecks.failure: Two men who do not like each other, and a camp that does not like strangers.

skillChecks.success: Three men across the street have stopped what they are doing to watch who talks to the sheriff. One of them writes something in a pocket book.
skillChecks.failure: A busy street on a cold day.

scenes.name: Prothero's Offer
scenes.description: On Tuesday, Simeon Prothero sends a boy to find the party. In the express office with the door locked he offers $5 a day each in dust for the week, $100 for every road agent taken alive and delivered to Sheriff Wyndham, and $500 shared if Thursday's boxes reach Bannack. He insists on 'alive' and 'the sheriff', and explains why without being asked: 'The company is not paying for hangings. The company will not have its money spent on that.' He shows them the waybill book if they ask. He tells them the coach will carry $38,000, and asks them to tell nobody. Benicio Aranda (or, if he is not played, an NPC messenger of the same name and sheet) will ride the box. The driver is Ike Leach, a weathered Ohioan who has driven the road since June and will drive it until it kills him.
scenes.readAloud: The express agent locks the door behind you and pulls the blind. He is a neat, small, grey-faced man of about forty-five with a pen behind his ear and the look of someone who has not slept in a month. 'Thursday's coach carries thirty-eight thousand dollars,' he says, 'and that is a thing I have told four people in this camp, and the last three times I told four people, the coach was robbed. I am now telling you, which makes eight. I need men on that coach who can shoot and who will not run, and I need them to bring me back the box, and I need them to bring the sheriff any man they catch. Alive. To the sheriff.' He looks at you over the counter. 'Not to the committee. I want that understood before we discuss money.'

skillChecks.success: He doubles the day rate and pays a day in advance, and lets you read the waybill book and his copy of the company's route instructions: the boxes are moved at Fiddler's Station 'for the convenience of the hostlers', a custom Sefton suggested in June.
skillChecks.failure: The terms stand. He is not a rich man and the company is not a generous one.

skillChecks.success: He is honest and terrified, and he knows people in camp are saying he is the inside man. He also suspects someone at the stations; he does not know which.
skillChecks.failure: A nervous clerk with a great deal of other people's money.

scenes.name: Supper at Moira Kehoe's
scenes.description: Moira Kehoe offers the party rooms, $10 a week with board. At supper, if anyone asks about the hangings, she tells them quietly and exactly what happened to Patrick, and where he was on the night of 2 to 3 November. Leonie Fairbairn, if played, is at the table; so, on Tuesday, is Gabriel Tennant, who leads the Methodist class meeting in the parlour on Sundays and comes by to see Moira. Gabriel listens and says little. A party that is kind to Moira and treats Patrick as a man, not a case, earns Gabriel's attention.
scenes.readAloud: The kitchen is warm and smells of soda bread, bacon and coffee. There are eight chairs round the table and one of them has been mended with wire. The widow serves you herself, small and straight and silent in a black dress she dyed in a washtub four days ago, and when she sits down at last she folds her hands on the table and looks at them for a moment before she eats. Somebody asks, as somebody always does. She does not cry. She says, 'He was down the Number Three shaft from six at night until six in the morning, with six men, and then he came home and slept until noon, and they knew it, and they hanged him at the gate anyway.' And then she says, 'Will you have more coffee.'

skillChecks.success: She is holding something else back, and it frightens her more than the committee does. (It is Davy Renner; see vg-scenario-002.)
skillChecks.failure: A grieving widow, and very private.

skillChecks.success: Gabriel Tennant, walking home with you afterwards, says: 'I sat with the first one. Tillery. The night before.' And then: 'Not here. Come by the forge.' (CLUE B1 is now open to the party: see act 3.)
skillChecks.failure: Gabriel says goodnight at the gate, courteously, and walks home alone.

acts.title: Thursday: The Rattlesnake Grade
acts.description: The coach leaves Ninebark at six in the morning, changes horses at Fiddler's Station at about nine, and starts down the Rattlesnake Grade at a quarter to ten. At the Elbow the road agents strike. This act is the scenario's set piece: let the players plan, ride, eat Sefton's stew and notice his washing, and then put them on a shelf of frozen road with a cliff on one side and a drop on the other, a rifleman in the rocks, and three masked men coming out of the timber.
objectives: Bring the coach and its boxes safely through the Rattlesnake Grade, or recover them
Take a road agent alive, if possible
Follow the tracks, and notice where they go
encounters: The robbery at the Elbow: Judd Ferrier (Gang Leader, masked, with his Army Revolver read as a Navy revolver), Hank Crewe and Davy Renner (Road Agents), and Wick Brill in the rocks above (Bandit Sharpshooter, half cover, 20 ft above the road). Nels Eklund watches from the ridge with field glasses and does not fight

A spooked team on a shelf road (combat.json mounted_combat and the coach's own rules): if the near leader is shot, the other horses rear and the coach slews toward the drop; DC 14 Animal Handling or Riding by the driver or a character on the box as an action to hold them, or the coach goes over the edge at the end of the next round, with anyone inside making a DC 13 DEX save to jump clear

scenes.name: Coffee at Fiddler's
scenes.description: Sefton is the perfect host: stew, coffee, a joke for every passenger, a question for every guard. He has heard about the party already, from the up coach on Monday, and asks the guards about themselves, their guns and their experience with friendly interest. He lifts each box himself as Jemmy carries them in. Outside, the washing hangs frozen on the line. Let the party notice it, or not; if anyone asks about it, Sefton laughs: 'Jemmy's idea of a joke. He washes when he's homesick.' Jemmy, asked, looks at the floor and says yes sir.
scenes.readAloud: Fiddler's Station is the warmest place you have been since Salt Lake City. The stove in the long room is red at the seams, there is a pot of venison stew on it the size of a washtub, and the station keeper is ladling it out with a laugh for everybody: a big, broad, ruddy man with grey in his beard and his sleeves rolled to the elbow. 'Guards! Good. About time the company spent some money. Sit, sit, eat. Jemmy, the boxes.' The hostler, a thin boy with a running nose, carries the green treasure boxes in from the coach one at a time and sets them by the door, and the keeper bends and lifts the first one himself by its handle, grunting, and sets it down again. 'Lord,' he says, cheerfully. 'Camp's luck is heavy this week.' Through the window, between the porch and the barn, two red flannel shirts and a red blanket hang on a line, frozen as stiff as boards.

skillChecks.success: CLUE D5. Washing, on a Thursday, in this cold: it will not dry, it will only freeze. And it is red, which shows a long way against snow. Benicio Aranda, if asked, remembers washing on that line the morning Will Danforth died.
skillChecks.failure: Frozen washing. A homesick boy.

skillChecks.success: When Sefton lifts the box, he is not joking. He is weighing it, and he is pleased.
skillChecks.failure: A generous man and a cheerful one.

scenes.name: The Elbow
scenes.description: Run the robbery as written in this act's encounters. Ferrier calls 'stand and deliver' from the road below the felled spruce, with his coach gun up; Brill fires from the rocks at the near leader as soon as the coach stops or the guards reach for a gun; Crewe and Renner come up out of the timber on the downhill side. The road agents want the boxes, not a fight: if the party makes it expensive (two road agents down, or the boxes clearly not coming), Ferrier calls them off, they go back into the timber to their horses, and Brill covers them. If Davy Renner is hurt he falls and is left behind; he is nineteen and terrified, and he is the most important person the party can take alive in the whole campaign. A masked road agent whistles 'Aura Lea' through his teeth while he waits; it is Ferrier (Benicio Aranda heard the same whistle on 13 October).
scenes.readAloud: The coach slows to a walk for the Elbow and the brake shoes squeal on the iron tyres. The road turns back on itself round a buttress of grey rock, and as the leaders come round it the driver swears and hauls them up: there is a spruce across the road, thirty yards on, its stump still white and wet with sap. In the silence after the horses stop you can hear the creek under its ice a long way below, and somebody whistling, quite softly, the tune of 'Aura Lea'. A man in a long grey coat, with a flour sack over his head and two holes cut in it, steps out from behind the spruce with a short double gun at his shoulder. 'Morning,' he says. 'Box down, hands up, and nobody needs to reach for his spectacles.'

skillChecks.success: You see the rifle barrel in the rocks above, before it fires. You act first in the round.
skillChecks.failure: The first you know of the rifleman is the near leader screaming.

skillChecks.success: The man in the flour sack looks at you, and at the guns on the box, and decides the box is not worth it today. He calls his men off before a shot is fired, and you get a good long look at his boots, his coat and a white scar showing through one eyehole in his left eyebrow.
skillChecks.failure: He laughs, and the rifle in the rocks fires.

scenes.name: The Tracks
scenes.description: After the fight, someone should follow the tracks: Ada Brockway, or anyone with Survival. The road agents led their horses down the timber from above, waited in a hollow sixty yards below the road, and went back the way they came, up the mountain toward the pass. If the party follows them, the tracks are lost after a mile and a half in the trampled snow round Fiddler's corral, and Sefton comes out on the porch, horrified to hear of the robbery, and tells them he saw riders cut across above the barn 'about noon' and took them for hunters. A cast shoe in the timber, with a toe clip, can go to Gabriel Tennant.
scenes.readAloud: Below the road the timber falls away so steeply that the snow has slid off the slope in places and lies in drifts against the trunks. The tracks are plain: four horses, led, not ridden, down a game trail to a hollow under a big fir where the snow is trampled flat and yellow with their urine, and the same four horses going back up, faster, ridden now, the hoofprints deep and splayed. They do not go down to the ford and the Bannack road. They go up. Up the mountain, through the timber, toward the pass. Toward the station where you ate stew an hour ago.

skillChecks.success: CLUE D2 (first half). The riders came from above and went back above, toward Fiddler's. Four horses: three men came down to the road, and one horse was led along the slope to the rocks above for the rifleman. One horse is lame on the off hind.
skillChecks.failure: The tracks go into the timber. You lose them in a blowdown; you can find them again with an hour's work.

skillChecks.success: A cast horseshoe in the snow by the hollow, recently thrown, with a small lip of iron turned up at the toe. Any blacksmith would know whose work it is. (CLUE D2, second half, when it reaches Gabriel Tennant.)
skillChecks.failure: Snow, needles and horse dung.

skillChecks.success: With Trailcraft or this roll: all four horses wear the same toe-clipped shoes, which is unusual for a gang of drifters. These horses were shod together, by one smith, recently.
skillChecks.failure: Shod horses. Most are, in winter.

acts.title: Friday and Saturday: Witnesses
acts.description: The committee wants to know what the party saw. The party wants to know what the committee knows. The point of this act is to put the party face to face with the machinery that made the list, and to show them how easily a name gets on it: the committee does not ask for evidence, it asks for a name. It ends with a card under a door, and, if the party has a prisoner, with lanterns coming down the gulch.
objectives: Give, or refuse to give, testimony to the committee without putting an innocent name on its list
Take Gabriel Tennant's account of Tillery's last night, and the cast shoe, to the forge
Protect any road agent taken alive until he can be put before a court
encounters: If the party has a road agent in the district jail: the committee comes for him at midnight on Saturday 19 November, eighteen masked men with lanterns and a rope (Lynch Mob, with Mordecai Pottinger as its ringleader), led down the gulch by Pottinger in a flour sack. Mob Mind: unmasking or arresting Pottinger breaks it at once; Barnabas Wyndham stands in the jail door with his shotgun and will not fire into it

scenes.name: Grimsby's Questions
scenes.description: On Friday afternoon, Horatio Grimsby, the camp's lawyer, invites the guards to his office 'on behalf of certain citizens' to give their account of the robbery. He is polite, precise and relentless, and he writes everything down. He asks about voices, accents, horses and boots, and he keeps steering: was the voice Southern? Missouri? Did the man in the sack say anything about the war? Pottinger sits in a chair by the window and says nothing. If anyone describes anything that could fit a person in camp (a Southern voice, a roan horse, a scar), Grimsby nods and writes, and that person's name will be on someone's lips by Sunday. If the party refuses to answer, Grimsby notes that too (WATCH +1). A party that turns the questions round and asks Grimsby who his 'certain citizens' are gets a thin smile and nothing else. Insight DC 13: Grimsby believes absolutely that what he is doing is lawful.
scenes.readAloud: Horatio Grimsby's office has a Turkey carpet, a safe the size of a small cow, a wall of calf-bound law books he carried over the mountains on two mules, and a fire. He is a slim, dark, clean-shaven man of about forty in a very good coat, with a soft voice, a steel pen and a sheet of foolscap in front of him. 'I represent certain citizens,' he says, 'who are concerned for the peace of this camp. You were witnesses yesterday to a felony. I would like you to describe, as exactly as you can, the men you saw.' He dips the pen. 'Let us begin with their voices. Would you say the man who spoke to you was a Southerner?'

skillChecks.success: He is not looking for the truth. He is looking for confirmation. Every question has a Missourian at the end of it. The man by the window, a heavy man with a Union rosette on his coat, is listening for one name in particular, and you do not know whose.
skillChecks.failure: A careful lawyer.

skillChecks.success: You give him a description that fits nobody at all, and he writes it down, and you have kept a name off the list.
skillChecks.failure: He catches you shading it, and looks at you for a long moment. WATCH +1.

skillChecks.success: He lets slip, as if it did not matter, that 'a confession was taken, under the most solemn circumstances, and names were given', and that the names are 'in this room'. His eyes go to the safe.
skillChecks.failure: 'The citizens' proceedings are confidential, I'm afraid.'

scenes.name: The Forge
scenes.description: Gabriel Tennant's forge on Water Street, late, the fire banked. If the party brings him the cast shoe, he names it at once as his own pattern, opens his account book, and goes quiet: he made that pattern only for the express company's string at Fiddler's Station, and shod them himself on 2 November. He does not say what that means. If the party has earned his trust (they were kind to Moira, they did not answer Grimsby, they brought a prisoner to the sheriff rather than the committee), he tells them about Tillery's last night: who let him into the cellar (Sefton, 'who was very kind'), and Tillery's words.
scenes.readAloud: The forge is the only warm thing on Water Street after dark. The fire is banked to a red eye, the anvil ticks as it cools, and the big man sits on an upturned keg with a Bible open on his knee that he is not reading. He takes the horseshoe from you and turns it in the firelight, and runs his thumb along the little lip of iron at the toe, and you watch his face close like a door. 'That's mine,' he says. 'I make them that way. Nobody else does.' He opens a ledger on the bench and runs a black finger down a column, and stops, and does not look up for a while.

skillChecks.success: CLUE B1. 'They sent for me the night before they hanged Jack Tillery, because nobody else would come. Mister Sefton was standing guard; he let me in and went up the steps. Near dawn the boy took hold of my coat and said, "The man said I'd live if I gave the names he gave me. He lied, didn't he, Reverend." I don't know who the man was. I told Mister Wexford. He told me to keep it to myself, for my own sake.' Gabriel looks at the horseshoe. 'I have.'
skillChecks.failure: 'I'll think on it,' he says. 'Come back Sunday, after meeting.' (He tells them on Sunday, in vg-scenario-002, if they come.)

skillChecks.success: He has seen the same thing you have, and he is afraid of it, because the man it points at is the most respected man on the road, and he is a Black blacksmith.
skillChecks.failure: A tired man at the end of a long day.

scenes.name: The Card Under the Door
scenes.description: At about two in the morning on Saturday 19 November, someone pushes a card under the door of Leonie Fairbairn's room at Moira Kehoe's (if Leonie is played; otherwise under the door of the Union Saloon's faro corner, and Leonie is an NPC lodger). It is a square of pasteboard, neatly printed in the Sentinel's type: LEAVE THIS CAMP IN TWENTY-FOUR HOURS. THE COMMITTEE. A party member awake in the boarding house hears soft footsteps on the porch, and can catch a glimpse of a man going away down the street: a heavy man in a long coat. It is Pottinger's barman, Clancy, sent by Pottinger. Ask Leonie's player before using this; the card is a threat, not a sentence, and the committee will not act on it for two weeks (vg-scenario-003), but she does not know that.
scenes.readAloud: You wake, and do not know why. The house is dark and very cold; the stove has gone out. Then you hear it again: a board creaking on the porch, under a weight, and the faint, dry whisper of something sliding across a floor. Footsteps, going away, unhurried. When you get to the window there is only a long coat and a hat, a big man walking down the middle of Water Street in the starlight, not looking back, and in the hallway, on the floorboards just inside a door, a small white square of card.

skillChecks.success: You follow him without being seen, to the back door of the Union Saloon. Mordecai Pottinger lets him in.
skillChecks.failure: He hears you and turns, and you both stand in the street for a moment; then he walks on. He knows your face now. WATCH +1.

skillChecks.success: The card is printed in the same type as the notice on Wexford's door. Jonas Fenley at the Sentinel printed a hundred of them on 5 November, on the committee's order, and will say so, ashamed, if asked in private.
skillChecks.failure: Printed. Anyone with access to a press.

scenes.name: Lanterns at the Jail (only if the party took a road agent alive)
scenes.description: Davy Renner (or whoever was taken) is in the district jail, a log cabin with one barred window, with Barnabas Wyndham and a shotgun. On Saturday night, Sefton, who has heard of the capture from the coach driver and is terrified of what Davy might say, urges the Executive to hang him at once. At midnight eighteen masked men come down the gulch with lanterns and a rope. Pottinger leads them. This is a Lynch Mob, and this time the prisoner is guilty of robbery, and he is nineteen. The party must decide what a guilty man is owed. The rules are clear (campaignRules: Hangings Are Murder): he is owed a court. If the party holds the jail without killing anyone, the committee loses face badly and twelve of its members never come out again; Sefton, who never goes to a hanging and is watching from a dark window of the Union Saloon, marks the party as a problem (WATCH +1). If Davy is hanged, the GM narrates it as the murder it is, and the party knows they let it happen.
scenes.readAloud: They come down Water Street at midnight, in silence, which is worse than shouting. Eighteen of them, perhaps twenty, with lanterns held low so that the light is on their boots and the snow and not on their faces, and their faces are flour sacks with holes cut in them, and one of them carries a coil of new rope over his shoulder like a man going to work. They stop in front of the jail. Behind you, in the dark of the cell, you hear the boy start to cry. In front of you, the sheriff steps into the doorway with his shotgun across his body, his spectacles catching the lantern light, and says, in a voice that shakes only a little, 'Gentlemen. Good evening. I know most of you by your boots.'

skillChecks.success: Mob Mind (adversaries.json Lynch Mob): the mob loses 2d10 hit points as men at the back slink away. Name a man aloud by his boots, his coat or his voice and it loses 1d10 more.
skillChecks.failure: The mob shifts and growls and does not leave.

skillChecks.success: As Persuasion. And if you pull the sack off the leader's head, or put him under arrest, the mob breaks at once: it is Mordecai Pottinger, and the camp will know it by morning.
skillChecks.failure: Someone in the crowd fires a rifle into the air, and the mob surges.

npcsInvolved.name: Barnabas Wyndham, 47
npcsInvolved.role: Sheriff of the Ninebark district; companion
npcsInvolved.description: A Latin master from Lancaster County elected sheriff by the miners' meeting; thin, stooped, spectacled, frightened and immovable. See his companion sheet.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Bring the robbers to a real court and stop the committee by law.

npcsInvolved.name: Simeon Prothero, 45
npcsInvolved.role: Agent of the Beaverhead Express Company; the party's employer
npcsInvolved.description: Neat, small, grey-faced, sleepless, honest. Refused to join the committee. Keeps the waybill book and the treasure in a brick vault. Suspected by Grimsby and Pottinger of being the inside man.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Get one coach through, keep his post, and see nobody hanged on the company's account.

npcsInvolved.name: Warrick Sefton, 44
npcsInvolved.role: Keeper of Fiddler's Station; committee number 23; the road agents' chief (secret)
npcsInvolved.description: Big, broad, ruddy, grey-bearded, sleeves rolled, a laugh you can hear across the yard. Knows everyone's name. Feeds travellers for nothing on cold days. Never rides on a robbery. Generous, funny, and completely without pity.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Keep the committee hanging the men who could identify his gang; rob the coaches; get away rich.

npcsInvolved.name: Obadiah Wexford, 58
npcsInvolved.role: Merchant; president and founder of the committee
npcsInvolved.description: Big, white-whiskered, prosperous, hospitable, a Vermonter who came west in 1849 and made his money selling flour to miners. Founded the committee because his customers' gold was being stolen. Frightened by what it has done since Kehoe.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Keep the camp safe and be told he was right. Can be turned.

npcsInvolved.name: Horatio Grimsby, 39
npcsInvolved.role: Lawyer; committee Executive; keeper of the list
npcsInvolved.description: Slim, dark, clean-shaven, a very good coat, a soft voice and a steel pen. A Philadelphia-trained attorney who has persuaded himself the committee is a court and its confessions are evidence.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Order, and the feeling of being its author.

npcsInvolved.name: Mordecai Pottinger, 50
npcsInvolved.role: Owner of the Union Saloon; committee Executive; the mob's ringleader
npcsInvolved.description: Heavy, red-faced, a Union rosette on his lapel and a flag over his door, an Ohio abolitionist who has become something worse. Sees a secessionist plot behind every robbery. Owes Leonie Fairbairn $1,100.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Drive the Missourians out; cancel his debt; feel like a soldier.

npcsInvolved.name: Judd Ferrier, 36
npcsInvolved.role: Road agent; the killer of Will Danforth
npcsInvolved.description: Tall, pale, quiet; a white scar through his left eyebrow; whistles 'Aura Lea' through his teeth when he waits. Wears a flour sack on the road and a long grey coat.

npcsInvolved.name: Davy Renner, 19
npcsInvolved.description: A thin, freckled Kansas boy who followed his cousin Hank Crewe into the gang. Took a pocket-pistol ball in the arm from a passenger on 20 October; it festered, and Moira Kehoe dug it out on 31 October, while Warrick Sefton paid for his room. Terrified. The key witness if he lives.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Not to die. He would give anything to go home.

npcsInvolved.name: Ike Leach, 52
npcsInvolved.description: A weathered Ohioan with a grey beard frozen white, a voice like a crow and opinions about every horse on the road. Has driven every robbed coach.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Drive the road, and not be shot doing it.

npcsInvolved.name: Jemmy, 16
npcsInvolved.description: A thin Kansas boy with a running nose who changes the horses and carries the boxes. Hangs the washing when Sefton tells him to and knows it means something. Terrified of Sefton and Ferrier.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Survive the winter. Could be the gentlest witness in the campaign if anyone is gentle with him.

rewards.money: Simeon Prothero pays $5 a day each in dust for the week (or $10 if bargained up), $100 for each road agent delivered alive to Sheriff Wyndham, and $500 shared if Thursday's boxes reach Bannack. If the boxes are lost he pays the day rate and apologises. A road agent's pockets hold $20 to $40 in dust each, which is evidence and should go to the sheriff.
items: The cast toe-clip horseshoe from the timber below the Elbow (CLUE D2)
Gabriel Tennant's account book entry: Fiddler's Station string, shod 2 November (CLUE D2)
Konrad Kranzler's notebook copy of Patrick Kehoe's true certificate (CLUE A3)
The committee's warning card from under Leonie Fairbairn's door
A road agent's flour-sack mask with eyeholes cut by a knife
Davy Renner, alive, if the party held the jail

twists: Warrick Sefton is the most likeable man the party meets this week, and the GM should play him that way without a hint of menace: generous, funny, interested, helpful. He asks the guards about their guns because he wants to know how many and what kind. If they tell him they suspect the station, he is shocked, then thoughtful, then helpful: he 'remembers' riders cutting across above his barn, and he offers to keep a watch. Everything he learns goes to Ferrier.

If Cormac Hartigan is played, Obadiah Wexford recognises his name from the list on Monday and is badly shaken; he does not know whether he is dining with a road agent or a marshal, and on Friday he asks Grimsby, privately, whether the committee is sure. Grimsby says yes. This is the first crack in the committee, and the party will not see it until vg-scenario-003.

Davy Renner, if captured, will not talk: 'They'll kill me. They'll kill my ma.' He is right to be afraid. Leave him in the jail; he breaks in vg-scenario-003 if the party has kept him alive and treated him decently.

Grimsby's interview is the first time the party can put a name on the list themselves. If a player describes a road agent in a way that fits an innocent man, let the consequence land in vg-scenario-002: that man's name is being whispered, and the committee has noticed.
dmTips: This scenario establishes the camp, the road, the factions and the mystery. Budget an hour for Monday and Tuesday, an hour and a half for Thursday's coach and the fight, and an hour for Friday and Saturday. The only certain fight is the robbery; the Union Saloon brawl and the jail are optional.

Run the robbery as a puzzle with guns: a shelf road, a felled tree, a rifleman above, two men below, and a team of six horses that will take the coach over the edge if they bolt. The road agents' aim is the boxes; they leave if the price gets too high. A good party saves the boxes and takes one man alive. A brilliant one also notices the washing.
Do not let anyone hang this week except by the party's inaction. The committee has hanged two men already and is pausing to see what the strangers do; the hook is the fear, not the rope.

If no one plays Cormac Hartigan, he travels on the Monday coach as an NPC deputy marshal (use his sheet), introduces himself to Barnabas and Prothero, and rides on Thursday's coach as a guard. He becomes the party's lawful ally and the list's twelfth name, and the GM can play him as the stubborn, plain, decent man his sheet describes.

If Leonie Fairbairn, Micah Garrick or Cormac Hartigan are played, their names are on the list. Agree with each player, before play, how much they want that to matter. The card under the door can go to an NPC instead.
Fiddler's Station should feel safe. The players will come to suspect it; let them get there themselves. Do not have Sefton do anything sinister on screen in this scenario.

Lynching appears only as a threat this week. If it happens, at the jail on Saturday, narrate it as what it is: a terrified boy, a botched knot, men who will not look at each other in the morning, and a sheriff weeping in the snow. Never as a payoff.
